mcq.q: Flowering and fruit set are most at risk in
choices: A A warm, still, dry spell
B Cold, wet or windy weather that causes poor set or millerandage
C A completely dry Mediterranean summer
mcq.answer: B Cold, wet or windy weather that causes poor set or millerandage
mcq.why: Coulure and millerandage cut yield when flowering is stressed.

mcq.q: A continental climate’s main ripening risk, besides winter cold, is
choices: A No sunshine at all in summer
B A short season and the chance of autumn rain or an early frost
mcq.answer: B A short season and the chance of autumn rain or an early frost
mcq.why: Hot summers, cold winters, and a compressed, risky shoulder season.

mcq.q: Downy mildew needs
choices: B Warm, wet conditions and is a foliar and bunch disease
mcq.answer: B Warm, wet conditions and is a foliar and bunch disease
mcq.why: Free water on the leaf; copper sprays are a traditional control.

mcq.q: Planting density is often high in the Médoc because
choices: A Vines then always yield more fruit per hectare
B Competition can reduce vigour and raise quality on fertile soils
C Machines cannot work wide rows
mcq.answer: B Competition can reduce vigour and raise quality on fertile soils
mcq.why: Many small vines, each carrying less fruit, is a quality tool — at a labour cost.

mcq.q: Hyperoxidation of white must is a deliberate choice to
choices: A Keep all thiols at all costs
B Brown unstable phenols early so the later wine is more stable to oxygen
C Start MLF in the press
mcq.answer: B Brown unstable phenols early so the later wine is more stable to oxygen
mcq.why: Used on some whites (often Sauvignon or less aromatic varieties); not for thiol-driven styles.

mcq.q: Punching down (pigeage) during a red ferment is done to
choices: A Keep the cap dry and separate
B Mix skins with the juice for colour, flavour and temperature evenness
D Remove all seeds on day one
mcq.answer: B Mix skins with the juice for colour, flavour and temperature evenness
mcq.why: The cap must be kept wet; pump-over is the gentler large-tank alternative.

mcq.q: Reverse osmosis or spinning cone in the winery might be used to
choices: B Adjust alcohol or concentrate flavour where the law allows
D Replace a cork with a screwcap
mcq.answer: B Adjust alcohol or concentrate flavour where the law allows
mcq.why: High-tech concentration/alcohol adjustment; not allowed or not used everywhere.

mcq.q: A white wine fermented in barrel, compared with one fermented in tank, usually shows more
choices: A Dissolved CO2 and no texture
B Texture, oak flavour and a broader mouth-feel
mcq.answer: B Texture, oak flavour and a broader mouth-feel
mcq.why: Wood plus a warmer, less reductive ferment builds body; typical of quality white Burgundy.

mcq.q: Saint-Julien is often said to sit stylistically
choices: B Between the perfume of Margaux and the firmness of Pauillac
mcq.answer: B Between the perfume of Margaux and the firmness of Pauillac
mcq.why: A compact Médoc commune with a high share of classified estates.

mcq.q: Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac, near Pomerol, are
choices: B Merlot-led Right Bank reds, usually less famous than Pomerol
mcq.answer: B Merlot-led Right Bank reds, usually less famous than Pomerol
mcq.why: Clay-limestone; value relative to Pomerol and Saint-Émilion.

mcq.q: Aloxe-Corton is unusual on the Côte de Beaune because it
choices: B Hosts the red Grand Cru Corton as well as white Corton-Charlemagne nearby
mcq.answer: B Hosts the red Grand Cru Corton as well as white Corton-Charlemagne nearby
mcq.why: Corton is the Côte de Beaune’s great red Grand Cru hill.

mcq.q: Bouzeron is a Côte Chalonnaise AOC for
mcq.answer: B Aligoté
mcq.why: The one village AOC dedicated to Aligoté; sharper than Chardonnay.

mcq.q: Jasnières and the Coteaux du Loir (north of Tours) make
choices: B Cool-climate Chenin Blanc, often bone-dry and high in acid
mcq.answer: B Cool-climate Chenin Blanc, often bone-dry and high in acid
mcq.why: Among the Loire’s coolest Chenin outposts.

mcq.q: Pouilly-sur-Loire, as opposed to Pouilly-Fumé, is a small AOC for
mcq.answer: B Chasselas
mcq.why: The town gives two AOCs; Fumé is the famous Sauvignon.

mcq.q: Saint-Péray is a Northern Rhône AOC for
choices: B Still and sparkling white wines from Marsanne and Roussanne
mcq.answer: B Still and sparkling white wines from Marsanne and Roussanne
mcq.why: Still whites plus a traditional-method sparkler; not a red AOC.

mcq.q: Lirac, beside Tavel, produces
choices: B Red, white and rosé in the Southern Rhône blend style
mcq.answer: B Red, white and rosé in the Southern Rhône blend style
mcq.why: A fuller neighbour; reds are GSM in outline.

mcq.q: Cahors is the South-West AOC for
choices: B Malbec (Côt), often firm and dark
mcq.answer: B Malbec (Côt), often firm and dark
mcq.why: The historic Malbec home; Mendoza made the grape famous later.

mcq.q: Edelzwicker and Gentil on an Alsace label indicate
choices: A A single Grand Cru Riesling
B A blend of white varieties, usually inexpensive
mcq.answer: B A blend of white varieties, usually inexpensive
mcq.why: Gentil has slightly tighter rules than Edelzwicker; neither is a Grand Cru concept.

mcq.q: Roero, across the Tanaro from the Langhe, is known for
choices: B Nebbiolo (Roero) and dry Arneis whites
mcq.answer: B Nebbiolo (Roero) and dry Arneis whites
mcq.why: Sandier soils; Roero Arneis is Piedmont’s friendly dry white.

mcq.q: Vernaccia di San Gimignano is
choices: B Tuscany’s historic dry white DOCG from the towered hill town
mcq.answer: B Tuscany’s historic dry white DOCG from the towered hill town
mcq.why: Often crisp and nutty; not Sangiovese.

mcq.q: Bardolino, on Garda, uses similar grapes to Valpolicella but is typically
choices: B A lighter, earlier red (and Chiaretto rosé)
mcq.answer: B A lighter, earlier red (and Chiaretto rosé)
mcq.why: Corvina-led; drink young; Chiaretto is the rosé.

mcq.q: Vermentino di Gallura (Sardinia) is a
choices: B Dry, aromatic white from a granitic DOCG
mcq.answer: B Dry, aromatic white from a granitic DOCG
mcq.why: Sardinia’s stand-out white; also as Ligurian Pigato / Tuscan Vermentino.

mcq.q: Calatayud and Campo de Borja in Aragón are sources of
choices: B Old-vine Garnacha, often excellent value
mcq.answer: B Old-vine Garnacha, often excellent value
mcq.why: Inland, continental, bush vines; ripe but can keep acid at altitude.

mcq.q: Getariako Txakolina is a
choices: A Full oaked red from Toro
B Pale, high-acid, slightly spritzy Basque white, often from Hondarrabi Zuri
mcq.answer: B Pale, high-acid, slightly spritzy Basque white, often from Hondarrabi Zuri
mcq.why: Atlantic Spain; poured from a height; drink young.

mcq.q: Valdepeñas, south of the Meseta, historically offered
choices: B Inexpensive Tempranillo (Cencibel) reds, some oak-aged in a Rioja manner
mcq.answer: B Inexpensive Tempranillo (Cencibel) reds, some oak-aged in a Rioja manner
mcq.why: La Mancha’s southern neighbour; volume and value.

mcq.q: Nahe Riesling is often described as
choices: B Sitting between Mosel delicacy and Rheingau weight, with mixed soils
mcq.answer: B Sitting between Mosel delicacy and Rheingau weight, with mixed soils
mcq.why: The Nahe is a small, geologically varied German region of high quality.

mcq.q: Nemea in the Peloponnese is the heartland of
choices: B Agiorgitiko, a supple red berry wine
mcq.answer: B Agiorgitiko, a supple red berry wine
mcq.why: Greece’s most planted red of quality; from pale and juicy to oak-aged.

mcq.q: Setúbal’s fame is split between
choices: B Fortified Moscatel de Setúbal and some Castelão table reds
mcq.answer: B Fortified Moscatel de Setúbal and some Castelão table reds
mcq.why: The peninsula does both a VDN Muscat and everyday reds.

mcq.q: Dão’s white wines often feature
choices: B Encruzado, which can take oak and age
mcq.answer: B Encruzado, which can take oak and age
mcq.why: Encruzado is Dão’s serious white; granite, moderate climate.

mcq.q: Columbia Valley and Walla Walla (Washington) are known for
choices: A Only foggy Pinot like the Willamette
B Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah in a dry, sunny, irrigated continental climate
mcq.answer: B Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah in a dry, sunny, irrigated continental climate
mcq.why: Rain-shadow desert viticulture; the Cascade barrier is the key.

mcq.q: Patagonia (Neuquén/Río Negro) is used in Argentina for
choices: B Cooler-climate Pinot, Merlot and fresher reds at high latitude
mcq.answer: B Cooler-climate Pinot, Merlot and fresher reds at high latitude
mcq.why: Southern, windy, long days; a contrast with Mendoza’s altitude story.

mcq.q: Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula are Victorian sources of
choices: B Cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
mcq.answer: B Cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
mcq.why: Port Phillip’s moderate climate; whole-bunch and restrained oak are common.

mcq.q: Waipara (North Canterbury) has a reputation for
choices: B Riesling and Pinot Noir in a sheltered South Island valley
mcq.answer: B Riesling and Pinot Noir in a sheltered South Island valley
mcq.why: Drier and a little warmer than much of the South Island coast; aromatic whites too.

mcq.q: A Spanish Vino de Pago is
choices: B A single-estate PDO, sitting at the top of the Spanish ladder in law
D A PGI with no rules
mcq.answer: B A single-estate PDO, sitting at the top of the Spanish ladder in law
mcq.why: Pago sits with or above DO/DOCa for a defined estate; rare.

mcq.q: If a Chilean label names a region such as Maipo, the wine must meet
choices: A No origin rule at all
B The national minimum (typically 75%) from that region unless a stricter claim is made
mcq.answer: B The national minimum (typically 75%) from that region unless a stricter claim is made
mcq.why: Chile’s standard geographic claim is 75% (variety and vintage often 75% too); some producers state more.

mcq.q: ‘Old vines’ on a label is
choices: A A legally identical term in every country with a fixed age
B Usually unregulated marketing, though some regions define it
C A PDO of its own
mcq.answer: B Usually unregulated marketing, though some regions define it
mcq.why: Lodi, Barossa and the Barossa Old Vine Charter are partial exceptions; most labels are informal.

mcq.q: A prestige cuvée Champagne is typically
choices: A The cheapest tank wine of the house
B A top blend or site wine, often vintage, with longer lees time
mcq.answer: B A top blend or site wine, often vintage, with longer lees time
mcq.why: Dom Pérignon, Cristal, etc.: selection + time, not a separate legal category.

mcq.q: Autolysis in sparkling wine contributes aromas of
mcq.answer: B Biscuit, bread and brioche
mcq.why: Yeast breakdown during lees ageing; the point of traditional-method time.

mcq.q: Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico is
choices: B A Lombard traditional-method wine, often Pinot Nero-based
mcq.answer: B A Lombard traditional-method wine, often Pinot Nero-based
mcq.why: Lombardy has Franciacorta and Oltrepò as bottle-fermented homes.

mcq.q: English sparkling wine’s grape mix is usually
choices: B Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier
mcq.answer: B Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier
mcq.why: Same trio as Champagne; cool climate on chalk or green-sand.

mcq.q: Brut Nature means the wine
choices: B Has little or no dosage (0–3 g/L) and no added sugar in the liqueur
mcq.answer: B Has little or no dosage (0–3 g/L) and no added sugar in the liqueur
mcq.why: The driest official band; only works if the base wine is ripe enough.

mcq.q: En rama Sherry is
choices: B A minimally filtered, often seasonal bottling that tastes closer to the cask
mcq.answer: B A minimally filtered, often seasonal bottling that tastes closer to the cask
mcq.why: More flor character and less stability; drink sooner, from the fridge.

mcq.q: Reserve Ruby Port, compared with basic Ruby, is
choices: B A selection with more concentration and length, still in a fruity, deep-coloured style
mcq.answer: B A selection with more concentration and length, still in a fruity, deep-coloured style
mcq.why: The first quality step up in the ruby family; not a vintage declaration.

mcq.q: Malmsey Madeira is
choices: B The sweetest classic style, from Malvasia
mcq.answer: B The sweetest classic style, from Malvasia
mcq.why: Rich, brown, high acid still; lasts indefinitely once matured.

mcq.q: Rivesaltes ambré or tuilé styles are
choices: B Oxidatively aged Roussillon VDNs (Muscat or Grenache families)
mcq.answer: B Oxidatively aged Roussillon VDNs (Muscat or Grenache families)
mcq.why: Colour words mark oxidative age; young grenat is the fruitier path.

mcq.q: Topaque from Rutherglen is made from
choices: B Muscadelle, fortified and aged oxidatively like Rutherglen Muscat
mcq.answer: B Muscadelle, fortified and aged oxidatively like Rutherglen Muscat
mcq.why: Once called Liqueur Tokay; tea, butterscotch and cut peel are the tropes.

mcq.q: Oxidation as a fault in a young white shows as
choices: A Pale lemon and fresh citrus
B Browning, nutty or sherry-like notes, and tired fruit
mcq.answer: B Browning, nutty or sherry-like notes, and tired fruit
mcq.why: Some wines are meant to be oxidative (Oloroso, some white Rioja); most young whites are not.

mcq.q: Sparkling wine for a reception should be served
choices: A At 16–18 °C in a small sticky glass
B Well chilled, opened without shaking, in a clean flute or white-wine glass
D From a dusty decanter of sediment
mcq.answer: B Well chilled, opened without shaking, in a clean flute or white-wine glass
mcq.why: Cold calms the foam; a wider glass shows a complex wine better than a cheap flute.

mcq.q: A high-acid, bone-dry wine with a creamy, fatty dish will typically
choices: B Cut the fat and refresh the palate
mcq.answer: B Cut the fat and refresh the palate
mcq.why: Acidity is the classic foil to butter, cream and fried food.

mcq.q: ‘Drink now, not suitable for ageing’ on the SAT means
choices: A The wine is too young
B The wine is at its best and will not gain from further cellar time
D The wine is too old
mcq.answer: B The wine is at its best and will not gain from further cellar time
mcq.why: Most inexpensive fruity wines sit here; it is not an insult.

parts.prompt: Contrast Napa Valley with the Sonoma Coast / Russian River Valley in climate and typical grapes.
points: Napa: warmer (especially east and north), Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, some Chardonnay; AVAs such as Oakville, Rutherford, Stags Leap.
Sonoma Coast / RRV: cooler, fog and breeze, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Both: Mediterranean in the broad sense, but mesoclimate is everything.
Mountains and fog gaps (Petaluma Gap, San Pablo Bay) as cooling tools.
Carneros (shared) as a cool bay-influenced zone for PN/Chard.
Do not treat all California as one climate.

parts.prompt: Describe typical winery choices for a Napa Cabernet destined for ageing.
points: Ripe harvest, sort, destem, ferment on skins (often warm), pump-over, extended maceration optional.
MLF; 18–24 months in a high share of new French oak.
Blending Merlot/Cabernet Franc for mid-palate.
Alcohol can be high; acid may be adjusted.
Bottle age after release.
Contrast with inexpensive Central Valley tank reds.

parts.prompt: What does an AVA guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
points: Geography: 85% of grapes from the named AVA (federal).
Not a quality tier, not a grape, not a yield limit, not a winemaking recipe.
Variety claim is a separate 75% (or higher in some states) rule.
A producer in Napa can still buy fruit from elsewhere if they do not claim the AVA.
Compare mentally with a French AOC, which ties grape and method to place.
County vs AVA percentages differ (75 vs 85).

parts.prompt: Compare Vinho Verde, Douro table wine and Dão in climate and typical style.
points: Vinho Verde: cool, wet, Atlantic; light, high-acid whites (Alvarinho, Loureiro), some reds; low alcohol, sometimes spritz.
Douro: hot, dry, schist; unfortified reds from Port grapes, full and structured; also some whites.
Dão: granite hills, more moderate, elegant Touriga-led reds and Encruzado whites.
All three are PDO table wines, not Port.
Vintage variation: rain at harvest on the coast vs drought inland.
Name grapes accurately.

parts.prompt: What vineyard factors allow the Douro to make both Port and serious dry red?
points: Same grapes and schist terraces; sugar and colour are high enough for either path.
Sub-zone: Cima Corgo quality heart; Superior hotter; Baixo Corgo wetter.
Dry reds need flavour ripeness without the safety net of residual sugar and spirit.
Altitude and aspect give fresher sites for table wine.
Old field blends.
Irrigation limits and low yields.

parts.prompt: Outline winemaking for a modern unfortified Douro tinto versus a Vinho Verde Alvarinho.
points: Douro red: destem (or some stem), skin ferment, extraction for ripe tannin, MLF, French oak common, 12–18 months.
Alvarinho: early-ish pick for acid, protective cool tank ferment, lees optional, little or no new oak, bottled young.
Do not fortify either.
Vinho Verde may retain a little CO2.
State style outcomes: full dry red vs light aromatic white.

parts.prompt: Describe Cava production from base wine to disgorgement, and the role of Reserva / Gran Reserva time.
points: Grapes: Macabeo (Viura) for softness, Xarel-lo for body, Parellada for delicacy; Chardonnay/Pinot allowed.
Early pick, whole-bunch or gentle press, tank ferment to a dry base.
Traditional method: tirage, bottle ferment, lees, riddling, disgorge, dosage (usually Brut).
Minimum lees time; Reserva and Gran Reserva (and some Paraje) are longer — more autolysis.
Most volume is Catalonia / Penedès; other Spanish zones exist.
Contrast with tank Prosecco.

parts.prompt: How do Cava’s grapes and climate typically set a different style from Champagne?
points: Warmer, Mediterranean vs cool continental Champagne — riper fruit, often a little lower in acid unless picked early.
Different varieties: no Meunier; Xarel-lo is a local signature (herbal, structure).
Many Cavas see shorter lees than vintage Champagne, so less toast.
Cost of land and labour is lower — everyday Cava vs prestige Champagne.
Top Cava de Paraje / long-aged wines close the gap.
Chardonnay/Pinot plantings move some wines closer to a Champagne flavour.

parts.prompt: Give service advice and a savoury pairing for a Brut Cava Gran Reserva.
points: Well chilled; white-wine glass if complex.
Drink on release or with a little bottle age; not a 30-year cellar project for most.
Pair with fried fish, jamón, or a mushroom dish — acid and bubbles cut fat; autolysis sits with umami if tannin is absent.
Avoid a dish sweeter than the wine.
Do not serve at red-wine temperature.

parts.prompt: List the cellar conditions that slow unwanted ageing, and two things that speed it up.
points: Cool (about 10–15 °C), steady, dark, humid enough for corks, quiet, on the side if cork.
Heat, temperature swings, light (especially UV), vibration, a dry cork, upright long storage with cork.
A working kitchen or a sunny car are bad cellars.
Screwcap wines can stand upright but still hate heat and light.
Humidity too high only damages labels, not the wine inside a sound cork.

parts.prompt: A customer says a white wine smells of damp cardboard and has no fruit. Name the fault, the likely cause, and what you would do.
points: Cork taint / TCA.
Usually the cork (or rarely cellar TCA); not the customer’s glass if a second bottle is clean.
Replace the bottle; do not try to decant it away.
It is faulty on the SAT — do not score quality as ‘poor but drinkable’ if TCA dominates.
Distinguish from reduction (struck match/egg, may blow off) and oxidation (browning, nuts).
Apologise; offer a different closure if the second corked bottle appears.

parts.prompt: Set a service temperature and glass for (i) Fino Sherry, (ii) village red Burgundy, (iii) vintage Champagne.
points: Fino: well chilled, white-wine glass, from a fresh bottle.
Red Burgundy: about 14–16 °C (not 20 °C+), a Burgundy bowl to catch perfume; decant only if sediment or very tight.
Vintage Champagne: well chilled but not frozen (about 8–10 °C), white-wine glass acceptable for a complex wine.
Do not serve Fino at room temperature or Burgundy ice-cold.
State why temperature changes the perception of acid, tannin and bubbles.
